📚 Reference Links

  • --write-out and the timing variables — everything.curl.dev: Write out

  • --resolve and --connect-to — everything.curl.dev: Name resolve tricks

  • Every flag, normatively — curl(1) man page

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Which -w variable is TTFB? time_starttransfer — DNS, connect, TLS and server think time are all inside it.
How do you get TLS handshake time alone? time_appconnect minus time_connect. curl gives no single TLS variable.
How do you hit one specific backend without editing /etc/hosts? --resolve host:443:10.0.1.7 — keeps SNI and the Host header intact.
-I vs -X HEAD — what's the trap? -I sends HEAD properly; -X HEAD on a GET-shaped command makes curl wait for a body that never comes.
Why does curl succeed where the browser fails? curl sends no Origin, no cookies, no preflight — so CORS and credentialed-auth failures are invisible to it.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

curl is the tool that turns "the API is slow" into a number with an owner. The --write-out timing variables split one request into five cumulative checkpoints — time_namelookup, time_connect, time_appconnect, time_starttransfer, time_total — so you can say "310 milliseconds, of which 240 was DNS" instead of "it's slow." --resolve then lets you re-run that same request against one specific backend IP while keeping SNI and the Host header correct, which is how you prove the load balancer is the problem rather than the app.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

The -w timing variables are cumulative, not durations. Why does that matter?

Every time_* variable except time_total is measured from the moment the transfer started, not from the end of the previous phase. time_appconnect is not "how long TLS took" — it is "how long until TLS finished", which includes DNS and the TCP handshake before it. To get a phase duration you subtract: TLS cost is time_appconnect - time_connect, server think time is time_starttransfer - time_pretransfer.

This bites in exactly the situation where you least want to be wrong. Someone posts a -w block in an incident channel showing time_appconnect: 0.310, and the room concludes TLS is slow. Subtract and you find time_connect was already 0.295 — TLS took 15 milliseconds and the problem is a slow DNS resolver or a distant endpoint. The subtraction is the whole skill.

The one genuinely independent number is time_redirect, which accumulates across all prior redirect hops, and time_total, which is the end of everything. If time_total is far larger than time_starttransfer, the server was fast to first byte and slow to finish — that is a body-size, streaming, or bandwidth story, not a backend-latency story.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

--resolve or /etc/hosts or just hitting the IP directly?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard follow-up whenever you say "I'd test one backend at a time."

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand that a modern HTTPS request carries the hostname in three separate places, and that two of the three approaches break at least one of them.

Hitting the IP directly — curl https://10.0.1.7/health — changes the SNI to the IP, changes the Host header to the IP, and fails certificate validation. You then reach for -k to silence the certificate error, and now you are testing a code path that does not exist in production: no SNI-based routing, no virtual-host selection, no certificate check. Half the interesting failures live in exactly those three things.

--resolve example.com:443:10.0.1.7 is the correct tool. It injects an entry into curl's own DNS cache for this invocation only, so the hostname stays the hostname everywhere it matters: SNI is example.com, the Host header is example.com, and the certificate validates normally. Nothing on the machine changes and nothing leaks into the next command.

/etc/hosts gets the same semantics but with global, persistent blast radius — it affects every process on the box, it survives your session, and it is the classic cause of "why is staging resolving to prod on Dave's laptop three weeks later." Use --resolve for a test, --connect-to when you need to redirect a host and port pair, and /etc/hosts essentially never.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

You run the same curl in a loop and the numbers get better after the first request. What is happening, and what does that hide?

The obvious part is caching: the resolver caches the DNS answer, so time_namelookup collapses from tens of milliseconds to near zero on every subsequent run. The less obvious part is TLS session resumption — if the server issues a session ticket, curl within one invocation may reuse it, and your OS or the intermediate proxy may too, which quietly removes a round trip from time_appconnect.

What this hides is the cold-start cost that your actual users pay. A browser opening your site for the first time, a mobile client waking from background, a Lambda on a cold container, a pod that just started — all of them pay full DNS plus TCP plus TLS. Benchmarking with a warm loop and reporting the median is how a team convinces itself that p50 is the story when the complaint is about p99 and first-visit latency.

The failure presents as a disagreement between two dashboards. Your synthetic check, which runs continuously and is permanently warm, shows a flat 40 milliseconds. Real-user monitoring shows a bimodal distribution with a second hump at 300 milliseconds. The gap between them is exactly the setup cost, and the way to reproduce it deliberately is a fresh curl per iteration with --no-keepalive and, where you can, a resolver flush — measuring the cold path on purpose rather than by accident.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

A customer says "your streaming endpoint is slow in Frankfurt." You have curl, shell access, and thirty minutes. What do you do?

🎯 Really testing: whether you decompose the path before touching any component, and whether you know which hops curl can see and which it cannot.

Start with the constraint that matters most: "slow" is undefined until it is split. The first command is a single curl -w run from a Frankfurt box against the production hostname, because that one output already partitions the problem into resolver, transport, TLS, backend think time, and body transfer. If time_namelookup dominates, this is a DNS story and none of the application hops matter. If time_starttransfer - time_pretransfer dominates, the network is fine and the backend is the answer. Thirty minutes is enough only because that one command eliminates four of five suspects.

Then walk the hops deliberately. The path is client → resolver → edge or CDN → regional load balancer → gateway → service, and curl can isolate most of it: --resolve pins a specific edge IP so you can compare two POPs; running the same command from inside the VPC removes the internet and the edge entirely; running it against the pod IP removes the load balancer. Each removal is a bisection. For a streaming endpoint the decisive extra measurement is time_starttransfer versus time_total — a healthy stream has a small first-byte time and a long total, and if time_starttransfer is close to time_total some hop is buffering the whole response before releasing it, which is a proxy configuration problem and not a latency problem at all.

The failure mode I would monitor first is the one curl cannot see: per-hop queueing under concurrency. A single curl is a single request on an idle path, so it will happily report 40 milliseconds while real traffic sits behind a saturated connection pool. Once the single-request path is proven clean, the question becomes load-dependent, and the tool changes from curl to connection-pool saturation and queue-depth metrics at each hop — which is exactly the handoff to Item 166.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Idiom What it isolates Use it when Watch out for
-w '%{time_*}' Which phase owns the latency Any "it's slow" report, as the first command Values are cumulative — subtract to get durations
--resolve One specific backend, hostname intact Suspecting one bad instance behind an LB Needs the port; --connect-to if the port also changes
-v / --trace-ascii Headers, redirects, negotiated TLS and ALPN Wrong content, wrong version, wrong route -v writes to stderr — remember 2>&1 when piping
-I Headers only, no body Cache headers, Content-Length, existence checks Some servers handle HEAD differently from GET
--http1.1 / --http2 / --http3 Whether the version is the problem gRPC or streaming misbehaving through a proxy Requires a curl built with the relevant backend
-k Nothing — it removes a check Almost never in diagnosis Hides the certificate failure that was the actual bug

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The five checkpoints are not curl's invention — they are the observable boundaries of the connection lifecycle, which is why the same split appears in the browser's Network panel (Item 164) and in any RED-style latency breakdown (Item 166).

Stage by stage, and where the round trips go.

time_namelookup ends when the resolver answers. This costs zero round trips on a cache hit and one to several on a miss, because a cold recursive resolution walks root → TLD → authoritative. It is the phase most likely to be invisible in your application metrics, because it happens before any of your instrumentation runs.

time_connect ends when the TCP handshake completes — one round trip after the address is known. Subtracting time_namelookup from it gives you a clean single-RTT measurement of the path, which is the closest thing to a ping you get without ICMP being allowed.

time_appconnect ends when TLS completes. With TLS 1.3 that is one additional round trip, so time_appconnect - time_connect ≈ 1 RTT on a healthy path; if it is materially more than the time_connect - time_namelookup figure, something is wrong — an expensive key exchange, an OCSP fetch, or a certificate chain large enough to need extra segments.

time_pretransfer is the point where curl has finished setup and is about to send the request; on a plain request it sits essentially on top of time_appconnect. Its value is as the subtrahend: time_starttransfer - time_pretransfer is server think time plus one network leg, and that is the number to hand to the backend team.

time_total - time_starttransfer is body transfer. For a normal JSON response it is near zero. For a streaming response it is the whole generation, which is why the streaming health check is "is time_starttransfer small while time_total is large" rather than any single number.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable this moves is mean time to the right team. Most latency incidents burn their first twenty minutes on the question of whose problem it is, and the honest answer is usually unavailable because the only number anyone has is end-to-end. One curl -w run replaces that argument with a partition: DNS, path, TLS, backend, transfer. Whoever owns the biggest slice owns the incident.

It also matters because it is the only latency measurement that is trivially reproducible by the person you are arguing with. A Grafana panel invites debate about the query, the aggregation window, and whether the exporter is lying. A one-line command with its output pasted underneath does not — the other side can run the identical command and either reproduce your number or discover the difference, and the difference is itself the finding ("it's fast from inside the VPC" is a complete diagnosis of an edge problem).

8. Command / Config / Code Example

The timing format is worth keeping in a file so you never retype it — this is the single most reusable artifact in this section.

# ~/.curl-format.txt  — cumulative checkpoints, newest at the bottom
cat > ~/.curl-format.txt <<'FMT'
     dns_resolution:  %{time_namelookup}s
       tcp_connect:   %{time_connect}s      # includes dns
       tls_handshake: %{time_appconnect}s   # includes dns + tcp
       pre_transfer:  %{time_pretransfer}s  # request about to be sent
       first_byte:    %{time_starttransfer}s  # TTFB
       total:         %{time_total}s
       http_version:  %{http_version}   size: %{size_download} bytes
       status:        %{http_code}      remote: %{remote_ip}:%{remote_port}
FMT

# The everyday invocation.
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "@$HOME/.curl-format.txt" https://api.example.com/v1/health
#     │  │  │
#     │  │  └─ discard the body; we want timings, not output
#     │  └──── -S keeps errors visible even though -s silences the progress meter
#     └─────── silent progress meter, or it pollutes the timing output

# Pin one backend behind the load balancer, hostname and SNI unchanged.
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "@$HOME/.curl-format.txt" \
     --resolve api.example.com:443:10.0.1.7 \
     https://api.example.com/v1/health

# Is the HTTP version the problem? Force each and compare TTFB.
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer}\n' --http1.1 https://api.example.com/v1/health
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer}\n' --http2   https://api.example.com/v1/health

# Is a hop buffering the stream? Watch bytes arrive against the clock.
curl -N -sS https://api.example.com/v1/chat -d '{"stream":true}' -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  | while IFS= read -r line; do printf '%s  %s\n' "$(date +%T.%3N)" "$line"; done
#      └─ -N disables curl's own output buffering; without it you are timing curl, not the server

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Real output from the second invocation above, run against a cross-region endpoint on a cold connection:

     dns_resolution:  0.241382s
       tcp_connect:   0.279117s
       tls_handshake: 0.318604s
       pre_transfer:  0.318741s
       first_byte:    0.401255s
       total:         0.403889s
       http_version:  2   size: 118 bytes
       status:        200  remote: 10.0.1.7:443

📥 curl starts                                              t = 0
    │
    ▼
🔍 [1] DNS resolution                    241 ms   ⚠️  60% of the whole request
    │      cold recursive lookup; cached runs show ~1 ms here
    ▼
🔗 [2] TCP handshake            +38 ms → 279 ms   ✅ one RTT, path is ~38 ms
    │
    ▼
🔒 [3] TLS 1.3 handshake        +39 ms → 319 ms   ✅ one RTT, matches the TCP leg
    │
    ▼
⚙️ [4] Server think + one leg   +83 ms → 401 ms   ✅ ≈ 45 ms of real work
    │
    ▼
🎯 [5] Body transfer             +3 ms → 404 ms   ✅ 118 bytes, negligible

1 — DNS owns the request. 241 milliseconds against a 38-millisecond network RTT means this was not one lookup; it was a cold recursive walk, or a resolver that failed over. Nothing downstream is worth investigating until this is explained, and no amount of backend optimisation will move the user-visible number while it stands.

2 — The transport is healthy. 279 - 241 = 38 ms for the TCP handshake is one clean round trip, and it gives you the path RTT for free — every later subtraction can be sanity-checked against it.

3 — TLS costs exactly one RTT, as TLS 1.3 should. 319 - 279 = 39 ms, within a millisecond of the TCP leg. Had this come back at 120 milliseconds, the suspects would be an oversized certificate chain or a synchronous revocation check, not "TLS is expensive."

4 — Server think time is the only application number here. 401 - 319 = 83 ms, of which roughly one network leg (~19 ms, half the RTT) is transit, leaving about 45 milliseconds of actual server work. That is the number to quote to the backend team — not the 404 millisecond total, which would send them chasing a problem they do not own.

5 — The body is free. A 118-byte response finishes 3 milliseconds after the first byte. For a streaming endpoint this line is the interesting one: seeing total sit within a few milliseconds of first_byte on a response that should have streamed for ten seconds is the signature of a buffering proxy, and it is visible in this output before you open a single config file.

10. When TO Use This

  • As the very first command of any latency investigation, before opening a dashboard. It costs one second and eliminates four of the five candidate owners.

  • When you need to prove which of N backends is bad. --resolve against each instance IP in turn, same hostname, same path — the one with the outlying time_starttransfer is your answer, and you found it without touching the load balancer's config.

  • When a client and a server disagree about what was sent. -v shows the exact request line, every header curl emitted, the negotiated ALPN and TLS version, and every redirect hop. That settles most "the API is broken" reports in one paste.

  • When you suspect a hop is buffering a stream. The time_starttransfer versus time_total gap is the cleanest available test, and -N makes it trustworthy by removing curl's own buffering from the measurement.

  • In a health-check or synthetic-monitoring script, where the -w variables give you a per-phase time series rather than a single opaque latency number — the same decomposition, but continuous.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not use curl to decide whether a browser request will work. curl sends no Origin, runs no preflight, applies no SameSite cookie rules, and enforces no mixed-content policy. A CORS failure is completely invisible to curl, which is why "but it works in curl" is one of the most misleading sentences in a debugging session. When the reporter is a browser, the tool is the browser (Item 164).

  • Do not report a single curl run as a latency measurement. One sample on an idle path tells you about the path, not about the service under load. Anything you plan to say out loud about p99 needs either many samples or a real load tool — curl diagnoses, it does not benchmark.

  • Do not reach for -k during diagnosis. It converts a precise, actionable certificate error — wrong SAN, expired intermediate, missing chain, SNI not matching — into a silent success, and you will spend the next hour on the wrong layer. If a certificate error appears, that is the finding.

  • Do not use it once concurrency is the suspect. A single request never queues, so curl will report a clean path while production is stalled behind an exhausted connection pool. At that point the question is queue depth and pool saturation, not per-request timing.

  • Do not use -X HEAD when you mean -I. -I sets the method and tells curl not to expect a body; -X only overrides the method string, so curl waits for a body the server correctly never sends, and the command hangs until it times out. It looks exactly like a server problem and is not one.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "time_appconnect is how long TLS took."

✅ Reality: Every time_* value except time_total is measured from t=0, so time_appconnect includes DNS and the TCP handshake. TLS cost is time_appconnect - time_connect. Reading the raw value as a phase duration reliably blames TLS for a slow resolver.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "curl https://<ip> with -k is the same test as the real request, minus the certificate check."

✅ Reality: It is a different request in three ways that matter — SNI becomes the IP, the Host header becomes the IP, and certificate validation is skipped. Any SNI-based routing, virtual-host selection, or certificate problem is now untestable, and those are exactly the failures you were trying to find. --resolve gives you the specific backend while keeping all three correct.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Quoting time_total and stopping. The total is the number the customer already gave you; the value you add is the split. Saying "404 milliseconds" is restating the complaint. Saying "404, of which 241 is DNS and 45 is the app" is a diagnosis, and it names an owner.

Naming the tool instead of the measurement. "I'd curl it" is not an answer. Which flags, which variable, and what would each possible result rule out? The senior engineer is testing whether you have a decision tree behind the command or just a reflex.

Forgetting that the first run is not the steady state. Presenting a warm-loop median as the user experience, or a cold single run as the steady state, are the same error in opposite directions. Say which one you measured and why it is the relevant one for the complaint at hand.

Ignoring the middle. curl from your laptop traverses your ISP, the edge, the CDN, the regional load balancer and the gateway before it reaches anything you wrote. Answering as if it were a two-party exchange skips every hop where the problem usually lives — and running the same command from progressively deeper inside the network is how you find which one.

Confident numbers with no source. "TLS adds about 100 milliseconds" is worse than useless when the subtraction in front of you says 39. This tool exists precisely so that you do not have to guess; guessing anyway, with the measurement available, is the trap.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Skipped — per the command-first rule, Section 14 applies only when the tool's own defaults are the point, and curl's documented defaults (connect timeout, keepalive interval) are not what this note turns on. The numbers that matter here are the ones you measure, and inventing citable constants for them would violate the no-fabrication rule.

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency A single measurement is exact but unrepresentative; many measurements are representative but take time you may not have mid-incident
💰 Cost Free, which is the point — the decomposition it gives you is the one thing an expensive APM often cannot, because APM instrumentation starts after DNS and TLS
🔒 Security / visibility -k buys you a working command at the cost of the diagnosis; --resolve gives you targeted testing with no loss of TLS fidelity
📈 Scale Single-request tooling by construction — it cannot see queueing, pool exhaustion, or per-tenant contention, which is where large-scale latency actually lives
🔧 Ops complexity Near zero, and portable to any box in the path, which is why it beats reproducing the problem locally
🐛 Debuggability The highest-fidelity view available at the HTTP layer without packet capture — but it stops at the TLS boundary, and below that you need tcpdump (Item 163)

16. Real World Usage

Every provider's own support playbook starts here. Cloudflare, Fastly and AWS support requests routinely ask for curl -svo /dev/null output with the timing block, because it disambiguates edge from origin in a single artifact — and the presence or absence of the provider's own trace headers in the -v output tells them which POP handled it.

The 2021 wave of expired-intermediate outages (the Let's Encrypt DST Root CA X3 expiry) presented to most teams as "our API works in the browser but our servers can't call it." The distinguishing evidence was a curl -v on an older box showing a chain validation failure while a newer box succeeded — a difference invisible to any dashboard, and instantly visible in the verbose handshake output.

Streaming LLM endpoints made the time_starttransfer / time_total gap a first-class check. The standard proof that a gateway is buffering token output is a curl -N where the timestamps arrive in one burst at the end rather than trickling — the same test described in Section 8, and the reason Item 168 in the AI section leans on this note.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • ../05-tls/ TLS 1.3 handshake note — why one extra RTT is the expected time_appconnect - time_connect

  • ../04-dns/ resolution-path note — why a cold time_namelookup can dwarf everything else

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 162-socket-state.md — when the timings look fine but connections are piling up

  • 164-browser-devtools-network.md — the same phase split, for the client curl cannot imitate

  • 167-triage-playbooks.md — where this command sits as step one of every playbook

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • httpie / xh — friendlier output, but no equivalent to the -w timing decomposition; reach for them for ergonomics, not diagnosis

  • openssl s_client — when the question is purely the TLS handshake, chain, or negotiated cipher and you want the raw exchange

  • wrk / vegeta / k6 — when the question is load-dependent; curl cannot answer anything about concurrency

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • dig +trace (Item 160) — the natural next command whenever time_namelookup is the outlier

  • mtr (Item 161) — the natural next command whenever time_connect is the outlier

  • Distributed tracing (Item 165) — pass a traceparent header on the curl and the request appears in your trace backend, joining the client-side split to the server-side span tree

19. System Design Application

Skipped — atomic tooling, not a system. Its architect-level treatment is discharged by the Section 3 Tier 4 follow-up, and the system-level story about which hop owns which slice of latency lives in ../14-performance-reliability/147-where-latency-goes.md.

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
dig says the record is correct but users still hit the old IP. Where do you look?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
You are cutting over a production hostname. What TTL do you set, and when?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • dig flags and output sections — BIND 9 manual pages: dig — DNS lookup utility

  • What the resolution path actually is — RFC 1034 §4.3.2: Algorithm

  • Header flags and RCODEs you will read in the output — RFC 1035 §4.1.1: Header section format

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does +trace do that a plain dig does not? Resolves iteratively from the root itself, ignoring your recursive resolver's cache.
Which flag in the output tells you the answer came from a cache? Absence of aa (authoritative answer) — plus a TTL that is not the record's configured value.
NXDOMAIN vs NOERROR with an empty ANSWER? NXDOMAIN = the name does not exist. NOERROR + empty = the name exists, but not for that record type.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

dig is the tool that answers "who told you that, and how long ago." A plain dig example.com asks your configured resolver and shows you its cached answer, complete with a decaying TTL — run it twice and the TTL drops, which is how you know it is cached rather than fresh. dig +trace throws that away and walks the delegation chain from the root nameservers yourself, so you see what the authoritative server actually publishes. The gap between those two answers is most DNS incidents: a record that changed, and a resolver somewhere still serving the old one until its TTL expires.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

dig says the record is correct but users still hit the old IP. Where do you look?

dig from your machine asked one resolver — almost certainly the one in /etc/resolv.conf, which is usually a local or corporate resolver. That answer says nothing about the resolver a user's ISP runs, the resolver inside the pod, the one their browser is using over DoH, or the OS-level cache on their laptop. DNS is a chain of caches, and you have inspected exactly one link of it.

The honest sequence is to compare three things: dig +trace for the authoritative truth, dig @8.8.8.8 and dig @1.1.1.1 for what large public resolvers currently hold, and the TTL on each answer for how long the stale ones will persist. If the authoritative record is right and the public resolvers are wrong, you are simply waiting out a TTL — and the remaining TTL in the answer tells you exactly how long. If the authoritative record is also wrong, you have a change-management problem, not a caching one.

The trap underneath this is that application runtimes cache too, and often more aggressively than the protocol permits. A JVM with a permissive networkaddress.cache.ttl will hold a resolved address for the life of the process regardless of TTL, which is why "we changed the DNS and the old pods still connect to the old database" is a recurring incident shape that no amount of dig on the host will explain.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

You are cutting over a production hostname. What TTL do you set, and when?

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand that TTL is a rollback budget, not a performance setting.

The TTL you set at cutover time is irrelevant — what governs the cutover is the TTL that was already published, because that is what every resolver cached before you touched anything. If the record has been sitting at 3600 seconds, the tail of your migration is an hour long no matter what you do next, and clients will keep arriving at the old endpoint for that entire window. The old endpoint therefore has to stay alive and correct for at least that long.

So the real move happens earlier: drop the TTL to something short — 60 seconds is the common choice — and then wait for the old TTL to expire before making the change. That is a two-phase migration where phase one is doing nothing except letting caches turn over. It costs you a day of planning and buys you a rollback that takes a minute instead of an hour.

The cost of a permanently short TTL is real but usually overstated: more queries to your authoritative servers, and a hard dependency on DNS availability at the moment of every cache miss — which is what turns a DNS outage into a total outage rather than a degraded one. My default is a short TTL on records that move (endpoints, failover targets) and a long one on records that do not (a CDN CNAME, an MX record), with a scheduled drop-and-wait before any planned cutover.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Command Asks Use it when
dig example.com Your configured resolver, cached answers First look; the TTL tells you cache age
dig +trace example.com Root → TLD → authoritative, iteratively You need the published truth, cache-free
dig @1.1.1.1 example.com One specific public resolver Confirming what the wider internet still holds
dig +short Same as plain, answer only Scripts and loops
dig -x 10.0.1.7 Reverse (PTR) lookup Turning an IP in a log into a name
nslookup Whatever it feels like Never, if dig is installed — its output hides the flags that matter

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Each arrow is a full round trip, which is why a cold resolution can cost 100+ milliseconds while a warm one costs under a millisecond — and why time_namelookup in a curl -w (Item 159) is bimodal rather than noisy. A plain dig collapses all three hops into one query to your resolver, and the answer it returns is whatever that resolver had left over from someone else's earlier lookup.

Two fields carry almost all the diagnostic weight. The aa flag in the header means the answering server is authoritative for the zone — +trace's final answer has it, a cached answer does not. The TTL on each record is the remaining life of the cache entry, not the configured value: run the same dig twice ten seconds apart, and a TTL that drops by ten confirms you are reading a cache and tells you precisely how much longer the stale answer will circulate.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# 1. What does MY resolver hold, and how stale is it?
dig api.example.com A
#    read three things: the ANSWER TTL (remaining cache life),
#    the flags line (no `aa` = cached), and ";; SERVER:" (who answered)

# 2. What does the zone actually publish? Cache-free, from the root.
dig +trace api.example.com
#    each block is one delegation hop; the last block has `aa` set

# 3. What does the rest of the internet still believe?
for r in 1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8 9.9.9.9; do
  printf '%-8s %s\n' "$r" "$(dig +short @"$r" api.example.com A)"
done
#    disagreement here = a cutover still draining, not a broken zone

# 4. Is the record even the right *type*? NOERROR with no ANSWER is not NXDOMAIN.
dig api.example.com A +noall +comments +answer
#    +noall then re-adding sections keeps the output to what you are arguing about

# 5. Inside a pod, the search list is the usual culprit — check it before the record.
cat /etc/resolv.conf   # ndots:5 turns `api` into five failed queries before the real one

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not treat dig +trace as what users experience. It deliberately bypasses every cache, so it shows you the published record and the cold-path latency, not the answer anyone is actually getting. For "what do users see", query the public resolvers instead.

  • Do not debug a container's DNS from the host. A pod resolves through the cluster resolver with a search-domain list that rewrites short names, so dig on the node answers a different question. Run it inside the pod, and check /etc/resolv.conf there — the ndots setting alone accounts for a large share of Kubernetes DNS confusion (Section 13).

  • Do not use nslookup when dig is available. It hides the header flags, does not show the TTL consistently across implementations, and its authoritative-versus-cached distinction is easy to misread. Every claim you would want to make from the output is better supported by dig.

  • Do not conclude "DNS is fine" from one successful query. DNS failures are frequently partial — one nameserver of four is stale, one resolver has a poisoned entry, one region's anycast instance is behind. A single successful lookup is one sample of a distributed system.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "The TTL in dig output is the TTL I configured."

✅ Reality: For a cached answer it is the remaining life of that cache entry, counting down. A record configured at 300 that returns a TTL of 42 means your resolver has been holding it for 258 seconds. Only an authoritative answer — the aa flag set, which +trace gives you — returns the configured value.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Lowering the TTL makes a cutover faster."

✅ Reality: Lowering it takes effect only after the previous TTL has expired everywhere, because caches are still holding answers stamped with the old value. The lowering has to happen at least one old-TTL period before the change, which makes it a planning step rather than a cutover step.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • ../04-dns/ TTL and caching-layers note — the several caches this tool inspects one at a time

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 159-curl-mastery.md — dig is the command you run when time_namelookup is the outlier

  • 167-triage-playbooks.md — DNS as the first branch of the "slow for some users" playbook

  • ../13-kubernetes-networking/ cluster-DNS note — where ndots, search domains and the pod resolver change the answer

notes.title: Path & Reachability — ping, mtr, and Proving a Port Is Open

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
ping fails but the service works. Is that a problem?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
mtr shows 40% loss at hop 7 of 12. Do you escalate to the network team?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • traceroute probe methods and why the default is UDP — traceroute(8) man page

  • mtr report mode and --tcp probing — mtr(8) man page

  • Why routers may rate-limit or not send the ICMP you are counting on — RFC 1812 §4.3.2: ICMP message generation rules

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why does traceroute show 100% loss at hop 6 but the destination still replies? That router deprioritises or drops ICMP TTL-exceeded replies. Mid-path loss that does not continue to the end is noise.
What does mtr give you that traceroute does not? Continuous sampling — per-hop loss and latency over hundreds of probes, so you see intermittent problems.
Cheapest proof that a TCP port is open? nc -vz host 443, or timeout 3 bash -c '</dev/tcp/host/443' when nc is absent.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

These three tools answer three different questions and are constantly confused. ping answers "is the host reachable by ICMP", which in a cloud environment often means nothing, because security groups routinely drop ICMP while TCP flows fine. mtr answers "which hop on the path is losing packets or adding latency", by running traceroute continuously and building a per-hop loss and latency table. nc -vz answers the only question that usually matters — "is this port accepting connections from here" — and that is the one to reach for first when the symptom is a connection that will not establish.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

ping fails but the service works. Is that a problem?

Almost never, and treating it as one is the classic junior move in a cloud environment. ping uses ICMP echo, which is a completely separate protocol from the TCP your service runs on. AWS security groups do not permit ICMP unless you explicitly add a rule; many corporate firewalls drop it wholesale; some load balancers do not respond to it at all because the thing you are pinging is a virtual IP with no host behind it. A failed ping to an ALB is the expected result, not a finding.

The inverse is the more useful and more surprising direction: ping succeeding tells you the host is up and the path carries packets, but says nothing about whether your port is listening, whether the process is healthy, or whether a security group permits your source. Plenty of incidents have "but I can ping it" as the sentence that wasted twenty minutes.

The rule I hold is that ICMP is a path tool and TCP is a service tool, and you should never substitute one for the other. If the question is "can I reach the service", the answer comes from nc -vz, curl, or openssl s_client — something that speaks the protocol the service actually speaks.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

mtr shows 40% loss at hop 7 of 12. Do you escalate to the network team?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can distinguish a measurement artifact from a real fault — because this specific output is the single most commonly misread thing in network debugging.

Not on that evidence alone. Intermediate hops report loss when they decline to generate ICMP TTL-exceeded replies, and routers are explicitly permitted to rate-limit those replies because generating them is control-plane work that competes with forwarding. A busy core router will happily forward your packets at line rate while answering only a fraction of the probes addressed to it — which shows up in mtr as heavy loss at that hop and zero loss at every hop after it.

The reading rule is simple: loss that does not propagate to the final hop is not loss. If hop 7 shows 40% and hops 8 through 12 show 0%, the traffic is fine and hop 7 is just stingy with ICMP. If hop 7 shows 40% and every subsequent hop shows 40% or more, that is real forwarding loss and hop 7 is where it starts — that is the escalation.

The second discipline is to probe the way your traffic travels. mtr --tcp --port 443 sends TCP SYN probes instead of ICMP or UDP, so the path you measure is the path a firewall and a load balancer will actually route, and hops that drop ICMP but forward TCP stop lying to you. When the destination is behind a stateful firewall or an anycast edge, the TCP-mode path and the ICMP-mode path can genuinely differ, and only one of them is your service's path.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Tool Probes with Answers When you'd actually pick it
ping ICMP echo Is the host answering ICMP, and at what RTT Quick liveness on a network you control; baseline RTT
traceroute UDP by default (-I ICMP, -T TCP) What the path looks like, once You need the hop list to hand to someone
mtr ICMP by default, --tcp available Per-hop loss and latency, continuously Intermittent problems — the only one that samples enough to see them
nc -vz A real TCP connection Is this port reachable and accepting from here Any "connection refused / timed out" report — this is the first command
openssl s_client TCP + TLS handshake Does TLS complete, and with which chain and SNI The port is open but TLS fails
curl -w The full HTTP request Where the time goes, end to end Once you know the port is open (Item 159)

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The mechanism behind every one of these tools is the TTL field: send a packet with TTL=n, and the nth router decrements it to zero, discards it, and sends back an ICMP time-exceeded message revealing its own address. Repeat for n = 1, 2, 3… and the replies assemble into a path. That is also the mechanism's weakness — you are measuring each hop's willingness to generate ICMP, which is a different thing from its willingness to forward your traffic.

Two consequences follow. First, per-hop latency is not additive and not meaningful in isolation: a hop showing 180 milliseconds while the next shows 40 does not mean that hop added 140 milliseconds, it means that router was slow to answer a low-priority control message. Only the final hop's latency is your real RTT. Second, the forward and return paths can differ, so a latency spike attributed to hop 7 may actually live on the return leg from hop 7 — which is why asymmetric routing makes traceroute output genuinely ambiguous and why the destination row is the only one worth quoting in an incident.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# 1. THE first command for "cannot connect". Port-level truth, from this host.
nc -vz api.example.com 443        # "succeeded!" = TCP handshake completed
timeout 3 bash -c '</dev/tcp/api.example.com/443' && echo open || echo blocked
#    the bash form works on minimal containers with no nc installed

# 2. Is it a path problem? Sample it properly — one traceroute proves nothing.
mtr --report --report-cycles 100 --tcp --port 443 api.example.com
#      │                   │        └─ probe with TCP SYN, the way real traffic travels
#      │                   └─ 100 samples; intermittent loss needs volume to show up
#      └─ non-interactive, prints a table and exits — the paste-into-a-ticket form

# 3. Baseline RTT, when ICMP is actually permitted.
ping -c 20 api.example.com | tail -2   # look at the stddev, not just the average

# 4. Port open but TLS failing? Next layer down.
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 | head -20
#                                              └─ send SNI, or you get the default vhost's cert

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not use ping to test a service. ICMP and TCP are different protocols with different firewall rules; a cloud load balancer that never answers a ping may be serving flawlessly. Use nc -vz or curl — something that speaks your protocol.

  • Do not escalate on mid-path loss that does not reach the destination. Routers are permitted to rate-limit ICMP replies, so loss at hop 7 with 0% at hop 12 is an artifact. Only loss that persists to the final hop is forwarding loss.

  • Do not run a single traceroute and call it a diagnosis. One pass is three probes per hop — nowhere near enough to detect intermittent loss, which is the failure mode you were probably sent to find. mtr --report-cycles 100 is the honest version of the same command.

  • Do not read per-hop latency as per-hop contribution. Intermediate latencies reflect control-plane responsiveness and the return path, not the forwarding delay a packet experiences. Quote the destination row.

  • Do not use these once the connection establishes. They answer reachability. If TCP connects and the request is slow, the tool changes to curl -w (Item 159) or socket-state inspection (Item 162) — path tools have nothing left to tell you.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Loss shown at an intermediate hop in mtr means packets are being dropped there."

✅ Reality: It means that router did not reply to your probe, which routers are explicitly allowed to skip under load — ICMP generation is control-plane work. Only loss that continues through every subsequent hop, including the destination, is real forwarding loss.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "ping working is a meaningful positive signal."

✅ Reality: It confirms the host answers ICMP and the path carries packets, and nothing else — not that your port is listening, not that the process is healthy, not that a security group permits your source, and not that TLS will complete. Every one of those has to be tested at its own layer, and each has its own tool.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • ../02-ip-packets-routing/ routing and TTL note — the field every one of these tools exploits

  • ../03-tcp-udp/ handshake note — what nc -vz is actually completing

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 159-curl-mastery.md — the next tool once the port is proven open

  • 162-socket-state.md — when the connection establishes and then misbehaves

  • ../12-cloud-networking/ security groups vs NACLs note — the usual reason a port is unreachable in a VPC, and the reason ICMP is silent

notes.title: Socket State — ss, and What Each State Is Accusing

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
Why is CLOSE_WAIT always your fault and TIME_WAIT usually not?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
Your client box shows 28,000 TIME_WAIT sockets and connections are starting to fail. What do you change?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • State filters, -i info, and the queue columns — ss(8) man page

  • TIME_WAIT, tcp_max_syn_backlog, and the tunables you will be asked about — tcp(7) man page

  • The state machine these names come from — RFC 9293 §3.3.2: State machine overview

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Thousands of CLOSE_WAIT — whose bug? Yours. The peer sent FIN; your application never called close(). A leak, not a network fault.
Thousands of TIME_WAIT — whose bug? The side that closed first, and usually not a bug at all — but it burns ephemeral ports on a client.
What do Recv-Q and Send-Q mean on a LISTEN socket? Recv-Q = pending accept queue depth; Send-Q = the backlog limit. Recv-Q near Send-Q means you are dropping connections.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

ss is the fastest way to turn "the service is unhealthy" into a specific accusation, because each TCP state points at a different owner. A pile of CLOSE_WAIT means the remote side hung up and your code never closed the socket — an application file-descriptor leak. A pile of TIME_WAIT on a client means you are opening and closing connections instead of pooling them, and you are on a path to ephemeral port exhaustion. A LISTEN socket whose Recv-Q is pegged at its Send-Q means the accept queue is full and the kernel is dropping connections before your code ever sees them. One command, ss -tan state ..., and three completely different investigations.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why is CLOSE_WAIT always your fault and TIME_WAIT usually not?

They sit on opposite sides of the close handshake. When a peer closes, it sends FIN and your kernel moves the socket to CLOSE_WAIT — meaning "the other end is done; I am waiting for the local application to close its side." The kernel cannot proceed without your close() call. So a socket stuck in CLOSE_WAIT is, definitionally, a socket your code forgot about: a connection not closed in a finally, a pooled client never shut down, a response body never drained. It sits there forever, holding a file descriptor, until the process dies.

TIME_WAIT is the mirror image and it is deliberate. The side that closes first holds the socket for 2×MSL — commonly 60 seconds on Linux — so that any delayed duplicate segment from the old connection cannot be delivered into a new connection reusing the same four-tuple, and so a retransmitted final ACK can still be answered. It is the protocol working correctly. It only becomes a problem through volume: a client making short-lived connections at high rate accumulates TIME_WAIT entries and eventually runs out of ephemeral ports for that destination.

That gives you two very different remedies. CLOSE_WAIT is fixed in code — find the path that does not close, and close it. TIME_WAIT is fixed in architecture — reuse connections (keep-alive, a connection pool) so you stop creating and destroying them, which removes the state rather than tuning around it.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Your client box shows 28,000 TIME_WAIT sockets and connections are starting to fail. What do you change?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard scaling question for any service that calls another service over HTTP without pooling.

🎯 Really testing: whether you reach for a kernel tunable or for the design change — because the tunables are the tempting wrong answer.

The arithmetic first, because it makes the choice obvious. The default Linux ephemeral range is roughly 28,000 ports, and each connection to the same destination IP and port consumes one of them for the TIME_WAIT duration. At 60 seconds of TIME_WAIT, a sustained rate above about 470 new connections per second to a single destination exhausts the range, and new connections then fail with EADDRNOTAVAIL — which surfaces in your application as a connection error that looks like the remote side is down when it is entirely local.

The tempting fixes are tunables: widen net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range, or enable net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse so the kernel may reuse a TIME_WAIT socket for a new outbound connection when timestamps make it safe. Both buy real headroom. Neither addresses why you are creating half a million connections an hour. (tcp_tw_recycle is the one to not reach for — it broke behind NAT and was removed from the kernel.)

The real fix is connection reuse. Keep-alive with a sized pool turns each connection into a long-lived one carrying thousands of requests, so the TIME_WAIT count collapses to near zero — and it removes a TCP and a TLS handshake from every request, two round trips you were paying for nothing. My order: fix the pooling, widen the port range as headroom, and treat a need for tcp_tw_reuse as a signal that the pooling is still wrong.

4. Quick Comparison Table

State Means Piling up points at First move
LISTEN Accepting connections Nothing by itself — but check its Recv-Q Compare Recv-Q to Send-Q (backlog)
SYN-SENT Sent SYN, no reply Firewall, security group, or dead peer nc -vz, then the security group
SYN-RECV Handshake half-open, in bulk Backlog pressure, or a SYN flood Recv-Q on the listener; tcp_max_syn_backlog
ESTABLISHED Working connection Only a problem by count — pool or fd limits ss -s totals against ulimit -n
FIN-WAIT-2 You closed; peer has not The peer's application is leaking Their side, not yours
CLOSE_WAIT Peer closed; you have not Your code — a missing close() Find the un-closed path; check fd count
TIME_WAIT You closed first; waiting 2×MSL No pooling; ephemeral port pressure Enable keep-alive / connection pooling

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The left branch is the active close — you closed first, so you pay TIME_WAIT. The right branch is the passive close — the peer closed, and the socket parks in CLOSE_WAIT until your application acts. That asymmetry is the whole diagnostic value: the state names tell you which side initiated, and therefore which side to go looking at.

The port-exhaustion arithmetic is worth being able to do out loud. Sustainable new-connection rate to a single destination ≈ ephemeral_ports / TIME_WAIT_seconds. With Linux's default range of about 28,232 usable ports and a 60-second TIME_WAIT, that is roughly 470 connections per second before EADDRNOTAVAIL starts appearing. Note what the formula does not contain: the remote service's capacity. This limit is entirely local, which is why it presents as "the downstream is refusing us" while the downstream's dashboards are clean.

The accept-queue reading is the other number in this output. On a LISTEN row, Recv-Q is the count of completed connections waiting for the application to accept(), and Send-Q is the configured backlog. When Recv-Q sits at Send-Q, the kernel is dropping new connections and the client sees timeouts while your application logs nothing at all — because the request never reached it.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# The triage sweep — one line per accusation.
ss -s                                    # totals by state; the 10-second overview
ss -tan state close-wait | wc -l         # your leak, if this is large or growing
ss -tan state time-wait  | wc -l         # your missing connection pool
ss -tln                                  # LISTEN rows: compare Recv-Q to Send-Q (backlog)

# Which process owns the leaked sockets? -p needs privileges.
sudo ss -tanp state close-wait | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

# Where are the TIME_WAITs pointing? One destination = a pooling bug for that client.
ss -tan state time-wait | awk '{print $5}' | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

# Per-connection kernel view: RTT, cwnd, retransmits — when throughput is the question.
ss -tin dst 10.0.1.7

# The headroom the arithmetic above depends on.
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range   # default 32768 60999 -> ~28k ports
ulimit -n                                    # fd ceiling: ESTABLISHED count cannot exceed it

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not tune TIME_WAIT away before fixing pooling. tcp_tw_reuse and a wider port range buy headroom, not a fix; the connection churn that produced the state is also costing you a TCP and a TLS handshake per request. And do not reach for tcp_tw_recycle at all — it broke clients behind NAT and has been removed from the kernel.

  • Do not read a high ESTABLISHED count as a problem. Long-lived connections are the goal. It only matters against a ceiling: the process fd limit, the load balancer's per-target connection cap, or memory. Compare it to ulimit -n, not to an intuition.

  • Do not run ss on the host when the socket lives in a container's namespace. You will see the host's sockets and conclude the pod is idle. Enter the namespace — nsenter -t <pid> -n ss -tan — or run it inside the container.

  • Do not use socket state to diagnose slowness. These states describe connection lifecycle, not latency. A perfectly healthy ESTABLISHED socket can be 900 milliseconds slow; that question belongs to curl -w (Item 159) and per-hop metrics (Item 166).

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "TIME_WAIT is a bug and should be tuned away."

✅ Reality: It is the protocol protecting a new connection from delayed duplicates of an old one on the same four-tuple, and from a lost final ACK. It is only ever a volume problem, and the volume comes from not reusing connections. Remove the churn and the state disappears on its own.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "CLOSE_WAIT piling up means the remote service is misbehaving."

✅ Reality: It means the remote service closed correctly — it sent FIN, as it should — and the local application never called close(). The state exists precisely to wait on you. It is one of the few network symptoms that is unambiguously an application bug on the machine you are looking at, and reading it the other way sends the investigation to the wrong team.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • ../03-tcp-udp/ connection teardown note — the state machine these names come from

  • ../03-tcp-udp/ sockets and ephemeral ports note — the resource the arithmetic here consumes

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • ../14-performance-reliability/148-connection-pooling-keepalive.md — the fix for almost everything this note diagnoses

  • 166-metrics-that-matter.md — turning these counts into continuous signals instead of a one-off command

  • 167-triage-playbooks.md — where socket state is the deciding check in the "intermittent connection resets" playbook

notes.title: Packet Capture — tcpdump and When You Actually Need Wireshark
notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Flags and the filter language — tcpdump(1) man page

  • Reassembling a conversation from a capture — Wireshark User's Guide: Following protocol streams

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The standard capture-to-file invocation? tcpdump -i any -nn -s0 -w cap.pcap 'host X and port 443' — then analyse elsewhere.
What does -nn do, and why always use it? Suppresses name resolution for hosts and ports; stops the capture generating its own DNS traffic.
What can't you read in a TLS capture? The payload. Without the session keys you get the handshake, SNI, sizes and timing — not the bodies.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

tcpdump is the layer below every other tool in this section: it shows the actual packets, so it settles questions that HTTP-level tooling cannot — whether a SYN ever left the box, who sent the RST, whether retransmissions are happening, whether the TLS handshake failed on ClientHello or on certificate validation. The normal workflow is capture narrowly on the server with a BPF filter and -w to a file, then open that file in Wireshark, where "Follow TCP stream" reassembles a conversation and the expert info flags retransmits and resets for you. You reach for it when the connection never reaches HTTP — resets, hangs, handshake failures — and essentially never before that point, because it is the most expensive tool here in both effort and disk.

notes.title: The Browser Network Panel — The Client curl Cannot Imitate

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
The waterfall shows most of the time in "Stalled". The server is fast. What is going on?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
"It works in curl but fails in the browser." How do you approach that gap?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Timing phases, the waterfall, and the columns — Chrome DevTools: Network features reference

  • The same phases as a programmatic API, for RUM — MDN: PerformanceResourceTiming

  • Why a preflight appears that your server never expected — MDN: CORS — Preflighted requests

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Long "Stalled" or "Queueing" bar — what does it mean? The request never left the browser yet: per-host connection limit, or waiting on a free socket.
Which column proves a request took HTTP/2 rather than 1.1? The Protocol column (h2, h3, http/1.1) — off by default, enable it in the column menu.
A request appears twice, first as OPTIONS? A CORS preflight. curl never generates one, which is why it "works in curl".

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

The Network panel is the only tool that shows you the request as the browser made it, which matters because the browser adds things no command-line client does: a preflight, an Origin header, cookie rules, a six-connections-per-host limit, and a cache. Its Timing tab splits each request into the same phases curl -w gives you — queueing, stalled, DNS, connect, TLS, request sent, waiting (TTFB), content download — so the diagnostic move is identical: find which bar is long. The difference is that two of those phases, Queueing and Stalled, exist only in a browser, and they are where a surprising share of "the API is slow" reports actually resolve.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

The waterfall shows most of the time in "Stalled". The server is fast. What is going on?

Stalled means the request has been created but has not yet been given a connection to travel on, so nothing about your server can explain it. Under HTTP/1.1 the browser opens at most six connections per origin, and everything beyond the sixth waits in the browser for one of those to free up. With twenty resources on a page, the last fourteen show as stalled — and the fix is on the client or the protocol, not the backend.

The two structural fixes are worth naming because they are the reason the HTTP version arc matters at all. Moving the origin to HTTP/2 collapses the six-connection limit into one multiplexed connection, so the stalling largely disappears. Sharding across multiple hostnames was the HTTP/1.1-era workaround for the same limit, and it is now actively harmful, because each extra origin costs another DNS lookup, another TCP handshake and another TLS handshake, while defeating HTTP/2's single-connection advantage.

Queueing is the neighbouring bar and means something slightly different: the browser deprioritised the request (a low-priority image behind render-blocking resources), or is waiting on a disk-cache entry. Both belong to the client. When either bar dominates, the honest report to the backend team is "this is not yours" — which is itself a valuable finding at 2am.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

"It works in curl but fails in the browser." How do you approach that gap?

📍 Seen in the wild: the most common false lead in any API integration issue.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know the specific list of things a browser does that a command-line client does not — vagueness here reads as never having debugged a real frontend.

The gap is a short, enumerable list, and knowing it converts a mystery into a checklist. The browser sends an Origin header and enforces the CORS response contract; it issues a preflight OPTIONS for non-simple requests and will fail the real request if the preflight's Access-Control-Allow-* headers do not cover the method, headers and credentials; it applies SameSite and Secure rules to cookies; it blocks mixed content; and it enforces Content Security Policy. curl does none of these. That is why curl succeeding is not evidence of anything about a browser request.

The panel is where you settle it, because CORS failures are legible there in a way they never are from the server side. The preflight appears as its own OPTIONS row directly above the failed request; select it and compare the Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers it sent against the Access-Control-Allow-* it got back. A missing Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, or an Allow-Origin of * on a credentialed request — which the spec forbids — is visible in ten seconds and invisible in any server log, because from the server's perspective it returned a 200 and nothing went wrong.

The honest engineering conclusion is that CORS is a server-side contract enforced by the client, so the tooling has to be client-side. When the reporter is a browser, reproduce in a browser; use curl afterwards to isolate whether the backend behaviour differs, not to decide whether the browser should have succeeded.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Signal in the panel What it usually means Where the fix lives
Long Queueing Browser deprioritised it, or disk-cache lookup Client — resource priority, fewer assets
Long Stalled Waiting for a free connection (6-per-host under HTTP/1.1) Protocol — move to HTTP/2; stop domain sharding
Long DNS Lookup Cold resolution, or too many distinct origins DNS / asset consolidation (Item 160)
Long Initial connection / SSL Distant origin, no connection reuse, heavy cert chain Edge termination, keep-alive (Item 159)
Long Waiting (TTFB) Genuine server think time — the only backend bar Backend
Long Content Download Payload size or bandwidth, not latency Compression, pagination, streaming
An extra OPTIONS row CORS preflight Server CORS headers (Item 167's "works locally" playbook)
Protocol column says http/1.1 ALPN did not negotiate h2 — often a proxy in between Proxy / LB config (Section 11)

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The right-hand group maps one-to-one onto the curl -w checkpoints from Item 159 — Initial connection is time_connect, SSL is the time_appconnect delta, Waiting (TTFB) is time_starttransfer minus time_pretransfer. The same subtraction discipline applies, except the panel has already done the subtraction for you and drawn each phase as its own bar.

The left-hand group is the part with no command-line equivalent, and its size is governed by a browser policy rather than by the network: six concurrent connections per origin for HTTP/1.1. With n render-blocking resources on one origin, the last of them cannot begin until roughly ⌈n/6⌉ - 1 earlier waves have finished, so stall time grows in steps rather than smoothly — which is why a page that added four images suddenly got a second slower. HTTP/2 removes the step function by multiplexing everything over one connection, which is the single largest practical win of the version upgrade for a page like this.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not use it as a latency benchmark. DevTools being open changes timings, extensions inject their own requests, and your laptop's network is not your users'. For distributions, use RUM built on PerformanceResourceTiming — the same phases, collected from real sessions.

  • Do not debug a server-to-server call here. Backend calls never touch a browser, so the browser-only phases are meaningless and CORS is irrelevant. That path belongs to curl, socket state, and traces.

  • Do not forget "Disable cache" and a hard reload. Half of "it's fixed" reports are a cached asset, and half of "it's broken" reports are a stale one. Without that checkbox the panel is showing you a history, not a measurement.

  • Do not read the throttling presets as ground truth. They simulate bandwidth and a fixed added latency, not packet loss, jitter, or a congested mobile radio — the things that actually make mobile slow. Useful for catching gross regressions, misleading as a mobile model.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A long bar in the waterfall means the server was slow."

✅ Reality: Only the Waiting (TTFB) segment is server think time. Queueing and Stalled are entirely browser-side, DNS and connection phases belong to the network and to your origin count, and Content Download is payload size. Four of the seven bars can be long while your backend is idle.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "If curl gets a 200, the browser will too."

✅ Reality: curl sends no Origin, triggers no preflight, applies no cookie or mixed-content policy, and enforces no CSP. A credentialed cross-origin request can return a perfectly good 200 that the browser then discards because Access-Control-Allow-Origin was * — the server sees success, the user sees failure, and only the Network panel shows both halves.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • ../07-http-semantics/ CORS note — the contract the preflight rows are enforcing

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)
