  • 167-triage-playbooks.md — the "works locally, fails behind the proxy" playbook, where this panel is step one

  • ../06-http-versions/ HTTP/2 note — why the Protocol column and the Stalled bar are the same story

notes.title: Distributed Tracing — One ID That Survives Every Hop

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
The trace shows the gateway span at 800 ms and the service span at 40 ms. Where did 760 ms go?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
What sampling rate do you run, and where is the decision made?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The traceparent header, field by field — W3C Trace Context: traceparent header

  • Traces, spans, and context propagation — OpenTelemetry: Traces

  • What a proxy does with request identity — Envoy: HTTP header manipulation — x-request-id

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The four traceparent fields? version (2 hex), trace-id (32 hex), parent-id (16 hex), trace-flags (2 hex), dash-separated.
Where does the sampling decision live? In trace-flags — bit 0 set means sampled. It travels with the request, so every hop agrees.
Why do traces break at a proxy? The hop dropped or regenerated the header. Unknown headers are not forwarded unless configured.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Distributed tracing gives one request a single identity that survives every hop, so a latency number stops being an average and becomes a waterfall you can point at. The mechanism is one header: traceparent, standardised by W3C as 00-<32-hex trace-id>-<16-hex span-id>-<01 flags>. Each service reads it, starts a span whose parent is the incoming span-id, and passes a new one downstream. The trace backend reassembles the tree from those parent links. Almost every "our tracing doesn't work" problem is one hop in the middle — a proxy, a queue, a background job — that failed to propagate that header.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

The trace shows the gateway span at 800 ms and the service span at 40 ms. Where did 760 ms go?

That gap is the most valuable thing a trace produces, and it is not time your service spent working — it is time between the parent span's clock starting and the child span's clock starting. Its usual owners are, in rough order of likelihood: queueing at the proxy or in the gateway's connection pool while waiting for an upstream connection; the TCP and TLS handshake to the upstream when no pooled connection was available; DNS resolution the gateway performed before connecting; and the network legs themselves.

The way you narrow it is by adding spans at the boundaries rather than inside the service. A client-side span around the outbound call — started before connection acquisition, not after — turns "760 ms of mystery" into "740 ms waiting for a pooled connection". Most tracing setups instrument the server side generously and the client side barely at all, which is exactly why the gaps end up unattributed.

Beware clock skew as an explanation. Spans carry timestamps from different machines, so small negative or overlapping durations are a skew artifact — but under NTP skew is milliseconds, not hundreds of them. A gap that large is real waiting, and the honest answer names queueing or connection setup rather than the clocks.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

What sampling rate do you run, and where is the decision made?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know that sampling is a propagated decision rather than a per-service config — the head/tail distinction is the real content of the question.

Head sampling decides at the first service to see the request, writes the answer into trace-flags, and every downstream hop honours it. That is what makes traces coherent: a trace is either fully captured or fully absent, never half. It is cheap, it is decided before any cost is incurred, and it has one fatal weakness — the decision is made before anyone knows whether the request was interesting, so at 1% you capture 1% of your errors and 1% of your slow requests, which are the only ones anyone ever wants to look at.

Tail sampling buffers all spans for a trace at a collector and decides after the fact, so you can keep every error and every request over a latency threshold while dropping the boring successes. It gives you exactly the traces you want, at the cost of a stateful collector that must hold spans until a trace is complete, plus enough memory and a timeout policy for traces that never complete. For a high-traffic system this is usually worth it.

My default is a low head rate for baseline volume — 1% or lower at scale — plus tail sampling that force-keeps errors and slow outliers, and an always-on override behind a debug header so support can capture one customer's request on demand. The cost is worth stating: span volume is request rate times services-per-request, so a 20-service path at 10k requests per second is 200k spans per second before sampling. That bill is why nobody runs 100%.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Concept What it is Confused with When it matters
trace-id 32 hex chars, one per end-to-end request span-id The key you search on in the backend
span-id / parent-id 16 hex chars, one per operation trace-id Builds the tree; a wrong parent flattens the waterfall
trace-flags Sampling bit, propagated A per-service setting Why one service cannot "turn on" a trace another dropped
tracestate Vendor key-value context alongside traceparent traceparent Multi-vendor propagation; usually ignorable
x-request-id A proxy's own correlation id trace-id Joins access logs to traces when tracing predates the proxy
Head sampling Decide at the first hop Tail sampling Cheap, coherent, blind to what was interesting
Tail sampling Decide at the collector, after the fact Head sampling Keeps errors and slow traces; needs stateful collectors

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Three invariants carry the whole design. The trace-id never changes along the request — it is the join key. The span-id changes at every hop, and the previous hop's span-id becomes this hop's parent, which is the only thing that lets the backend rebuild a tree from independently-reported spans. The flags propagate unchanged, which is why sampling is coherent across services that never talk to each other.

The two places this breaks are both boundaries where headers stop being automatic. A proxy or load balancer forwards unknown headers in most default configurations but not all — and a gateway that terminates and re-originates a request, or a Lambda-style integration that maps only named headers, will drop traceparent silently. An asynchronous boundary breaks it by construction: publishing to SQS or Kafka does not carry HTTP headers, so the context has to be serialised into the message's own attributes and re-extracted by the consumer. Both failures present identically — a trace that ends abruptly, and orphan traces beginning at the hop after the break, which is how you locate it.

The volume arithmetic is worth holding: spans per second ≈ request rate × spans per request, where spans per request is roughly two per service hop (one client-side, one server-side) plus any internal spans. Ten thousand requests per second across a ten-service path is on the order of 200,000 spans per second — the number that makes the sampling conversation unavoidable rather than optional.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not expect tracing to answer a "why is this one hop slow" question. A trace tells you which hop and how long; it rarely tells you why. Once it points at a service, the tools are profiles, connection-pool metrics and socket state (Item 162) — tracing has done its job when it narrows the search.

  • Do not run 100% sampling at scale and call it thoroughness. Span volume grows with request rate times hop count, and the storage bill plus the collector's own latency become a production concern of their own. Tail-sample errors and outliers instead of keeping everything.

  • Do not put high-cardinality user data in span attributes. Trace backends index attributes, so a raw user id or a full URL with query parameters becomes a cardinality explosion that is expensive to store and, for PII, is a data-handling problem in a system with broad read access.

  • Do not trust a trace whose spans are missing in the middle. A gap usually means a hop is not instrumented, not that the hop was instant. Confirm coverage before drawing conclusions from a waterfall — an uninstrumented service looks exactly like a fast one.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Each service decides whether to sample its own requests."

✅ Reality: The decision is made once, encoded in trace-flags, and propagated. Downstream services honour it. That is precisely what makes traces whole rather than a scatter of unrelated fragments — and it is why a service "enabling tracing" changes nothing if the upstream is dropping the header.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "The gap between a parent span and its child is network latency."

✅ Reality: It is everything between the parent starting its outbound call and the child starting to handle it — connection-pool wait, DNS, TCP and TLS setup, proxy queueing, and only then the wire time. On a healthy same-region path the actual network leg is often under a millisecond of a gap measured in hundreds, and instrumenting the client side is what makes the difference visible.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • ../07-http-semantics/ headers note — propagation is a header contract before it is anything else

  • 166-metrics-that-matter.md — metrics tell you something is wrong; traces tell you where

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 167-triage-playbooks.md — the trace waterfall as the "slow for some users" playbook's second step

  • ../11-proxies-load-balancers/116-api-gateway.md — the hop most likely to break propagation

  • ../14-performance-reliability/153-tail-latency.md — why the interesting traces are the ones head sampling throws away

notes.title: The Metrics That Matter — RED at Every Hop, Plus What Runs Out

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
Why is RED at every hop worth the cardinality it costs?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
What do you actually page on — latency, errors, or saturation?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The four golden signals, and why saturation is one of them — Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

  • The resource-side complement — utilisation, saturation, errors — Brendan Gregg: The USE Method

  • Where per-hop numbers come from at the proxy — Envoy: HTTP header manipulation and request identity

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does RED stand for, and what does it miss? Rate, Errors, Duration — request-side. It misses saturation, which is what predicts the failure.
Why is averaging latency across hops wrong? Averages hide the tail, and the tail is the user experience. Aggregate histograms, then read quantiles.
The single most predictive connection-level signal? Queue depth / pool saturation — it rises before latency does, which makes it the alertable one.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

RED — rate, errors, duration — is the request-side triple you want emitted at every hop, not just at the edge, because the value is in the differences between hops. When the edge reports 900 ms and the service reports 40, the missing 860 belongs to a hop in between, and you can only see that if every hop reports. What RED alone misses is saturation: connection-pool usage, accept-queue depth, in-flight requests against the concurrency limit. Those are the signals that move before latency does, which makes them the ones worth alerting on rather than merely graphing.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why is RED at every hop worth the cardinality it costs?

Because a single end-to-end latency number is unattributable, and attribution is the entire job during an incident. Duration measured only at the edge tells you the system is slow. The same measurement taken at the edge, the gateway, the service and the database turns that into a subtraction chain — each hop's duration minus its downstream's duration is that hop's own cost, including whatever it spent queueing to reach the next one. That is the metric equivalent of the curl -w split in Item 159, applied continuously instead of once.

Errors need the same treatment for a different reason: the same failure changes its identity as it travels. A backend timeout becomes a 504 at the proxy and a generic "network error" at the browser. Counting errors only at the edge tells you the rate but destroys the cause; counting them at each hop, labelled by status class, preserves the chain — a spike in upstream connect failures at the proxy and a flat error rate at the service is a completely different incident from the reverse.

The cardinality cost is manageable if you are disciplined about labels: keep the dimensions that support the subtraction — hop, route, status class, upstream cluster — and refuse the ones that explode. A label is acceptable if you can name a query you would actually run against it.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

What do you actually page on — latency, errors, or saturation?

🎯 Really testing: whether you distinguish symptom alerts from cause alerts, and whether you know that saturation is the leading indicator.

Page on symptoms, diagnose with causes. The pages should be a small set of user-visible conditions — error-rate budget burn and latency SLO burn — because those are the things that are true failures regardless of mechanism, and they do not need updating every time the architecture changes. A page for "CPU above 80%" fires during a healthy batch job and stays silent during a connection-pool stall, which is the wrong behaviour in both directions.

Saturation sits in between and is the genuinely valuable middle ground: connection-pool utilisation, accept-queue depth, in-flight requests against a concurrency limit, and socket-state counts (Item 162). These move before latency does, because a queue fills first and only then does waiting appear. That makes them excellent for a warning-level notification and for the first dashboard you open, but poor as a page on their own — a pool that touches 100% for two seconds under a burst is not an incident.

The saturation signals I would page on are the ones with no graceful degradation behind them: an accept queue dropping connections, or ephemeral port exhaustion. Those present as connection refusals that never reach application logs, so waiting for a symptom alert means waiting for a user. Everything else is a warning that buys you the twenty minutes before the page would have fired.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Framework Measures Point of view When you'd actually pick it
RED (rate, errors, duration) Requests The caller's Any request-serving hop — the default for services and proxies
USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) Resources The machine's CPU, memory, disk, NICs, connection pools — the "what is full" question
Four golden signals Latency, traffic, errors, saturation Both SLO definition; RED plus the saturation term it omits
Connection-level signals Sockets, queues, pools The transport's Networking specifically — where RED is blind (Item 162)

RED and USE are complements, not rivals: RED tells you the service is failing its callers, USE tells you which resource ran out. The networking-specific gap both leave is the connection layer — a service can be green on RED and USE while its upstream pool is exhausted, because the requests are queueing in a place neither framework looks at by default.

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The diagram is the method: 840 milliseconds appear between the gateway's own duration and the service's, and the saturated pool on the same hop names the reason. Neither number alone would have found it — the gateway's RED says "slow", the pool gauge says "why".

Why saturation leads latency is Little's Law plus the utilisation curve, and it is worth being able to state. In a queueing system, average wait rises roughly as 1/(1-ρ) with utilisation ρ, so latency is nearly flat from 0% to 70% and then climbs steeply: going from 70% to 80% roughly doubles the wait, and 90% to 95% doubles it again. Utilisation is therefore observable and nearly linear while its effect on latency is still invisible — which is exactly the property you want in a leading indicator.

Why you aggregate histograms, not averages, is the other half. Percentiles do not average: the mean of two hops' p99 values is not the p99 of the path, and averaging a p99 across ten pods is not the fleet's p99. Emit latency as a histogram, sum the buckets across instances, and compute the quantile from the summed histogram. Averaging pre-computed percentiles is one of the most common quiet errors in a metrics pipeline, and it always reports the tail as better than it is.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not alert on every RED metric at every hop. Per-hop metrics are for diagnosis; pages belong on user-visible symptoms and on saturation signals with no graceful degradation. A page per hop produces an alert storm in which the single real signal is invisible.

  • Do not average percentiles. Aggregate the underlying histogram and compute the quantile once. Averaging p99s across pods or across hops understates the tail, reliably and in the direction that makes you complacent.

  • Do not label metrics with unbounded dimensions. User id, full path with query string, or raw error message multiply time series without limit and will take down the metrics system before the incident does. If you cannot name the query you would run against a label, drop it.

  • Do not substitute metrics for traces. Metrics tell you that a hop is slow and roughly how often; they cannot show you one request's path. When the question is "what happened to this customer's request", that is Item 165's job, and no amount of dimensional labelling will get you there.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "RED covers what you need for a service."

✅ Reality: RED is request-side only and has no saturation term, which is the one signal that moves before users notice. A service can be green on rate, errors and duration while its upstream connection pool sits at 98% and is seconds away from queueing — the golden-signals framing adds saturation precisely because RED alone cannot see the cliff coming.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "p99 latency across the fleet is the average of each instance's p99."

✅ Reality: Percentiles are not linear and do not average. The fleet's p99 has to be computed from summed histogram buckets, and the averaged version is systematically optimistic — it smooths away exactly the one slow instance you were trying to detect.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • ../14-performance-reliability/152-queueing-theory.md — the utilisation curve that makes saturation a leading indicator

  • 162-socket-state.md — the connection-level counts these dashboards should be built on

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 165-distributed-tracing.md — the per-request view metrics can only point at

  • 167-triage-playbooks.md — the playbooks assume these metrics exist at every hop

  • ../14-performance-reliability/153-tail-latency.md — why the quantile you compute is the one that matters

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • What 502, 503 and 504 are each specified to mean — RFC 9110 §15.6: Server Error 5xx

  • Which upstream conditions a proxy converts into which code — nginx: ngx_http_upstream_module

  • Retry, timeout and backoff discipline behind the fixes — Amazon Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter

  • Bonus — the first command in every playbook below: everything.curl.dev: Write out

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Who emits 502, 503 and 504? The proxy, all three. 502 = bad upstream response, 503 = no healthy upstream, 504 = upstream too slow.
"Slow for some users" — first check? Segment before you measure: by region, by client version, by whether the connection is new or reused.
"Works in curl, fails in the browser" — first suspect? CORS preflight, cookies, or CSP — the things curl does not send.
Streaming stalls in prod but not locally — first suspect? A buffering hop. proxy_buffering, a CDN, or an ALB idle timeout.
Intermittent resets — which state do you count first? CLOSE_WAIT for a leak, TIME_WAIT for port pressure; then check idle timeouts on both sides.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A triage playbook is a symptom mapped to the two or three checks that partition the suspects, in an order chosen so each check eliminates the most candidates. For a 5xx that means reading the code as an accusation — 502, 503 and 504 all come from the proxy and each points at a different failure of the upstream. For "slow for some users" it means segmenting before measuring, because an average across two populations describes neither. The discipline the playbooks encode is that you eliminate whole layers with cheap commands before you open anyone's code, and the reason to write them down is that at 3am nobody derives them.

4. Quick Comparison Table — the playbooks

4a. The 5xx table — read the code as an accusation

Code The proxy is saying Common cause First check What it rules out
502 Bad Gateway "I connected but got garbage or the connection died mid-response" App crashed mid-request; upstream closed early; protocol mismatch (h2 vs h1.1); response header too large Upstream logs at that timestamp; proxy error log for the specific reason Rules out "no capacity" — something answered
503 Service Unavailable "I have no healthy upstream to send this to" All targets failing health checks; deploy drained everything; circuit breaker open; connection limit hit Target-group / upstream health status Rules out the app's request handling — nothing was tried
504 Gateway Timeout "The upstream did not respond within my timeout" Slow backend; deadlock; a downstream dependency slower than your timeout Compare the proxy's timeout to the backend's own p99 Rules out a dead backend — it was alive, just slow
500 from the app "The app itself failed" An unhandled exception in your code The app's stack trace Rules out the whole network path
499 (nginx) "The client gave up before I answered" Client timeout shorter than server time; user navigated away Client-side timeout config Rules out the server — it was still working
429 "Rate limited" Quota or per-tenant limit; a retry storm Retry-After, and your own retry policy Rules out a fault — this is policy

4b. Symptom → the checks, in order

Symptom Check 1 Check 2 Check 3 Usual owner
Sudden 5xx spike Which code, and at which hop emits it Deploy / config change in the last 30 min Upstream health + saturation Whoever the code accuses
Slow for some users Segment: region, client version, new vs reused connection curl -w from an affected region — which phase is long Trace waterfall for an affected request Whichever phase is long
Works locally, fails behind the proxy Browser Network panel: is there an OPTIONS row Compare request headers local vs deployed Proxy header/size/method rules Proxy or CORS config
Streaming stalls in prod curl -N — do bytes trickle or arrive in one burst proxy_buffering / CDN / X-Accel-Buffering on every hop Idle timeouts on every hop (ALB default 60s) The first buffering hop
Intermittent connection resets ss -tan state counts on both sides Idle-timeout mismatch: client pool vs LB vs server Deploy / scale-in events at the same timestamps Usually a timeout mismatch
Works for old clients, fails for new Protocol column / ALPN — h2 vs http/1.1 Header size, method, or Expect: 100-continue Proxy version and its defaults Proxy config

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Walk me through 502 versus 503 versus 504 without saying "server error".

All three are emitted by the intermediary, not by your application, and that is the first thing to say — it means the proxy formed an opinion about the upstream, and each code names a different opinion. 502 means a connection was made and what came back was unusable: the upstream closed mid-response, spoke the wrong protocol, or sent headers the proxy refused. Something was alive and answering, which is why 502 rules out a capacity problem.

503 means the proxy had nowhere to send the request. Every target failed its health check, or a deploy drained the pool, or a connection limit was reached. The request was never attempted upstream, so no application log will contain it — which is a useful negative signal in itself: a 503 spike with silent application logs is consistent, not mysterious.

504 means the upstream was reachable and accepted the request but did not answer within the proxy's read timeout. The backend is alive and slow, so the code is really a statement about the relationship between two numbers — the proxy's timeout and the backend's actual p99. That is why a 504 is so often fixed at the wrong layer: raising the proxy timeout converts a fast failure into a slow one and hides the regression, without making anything faster.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

A 504 spike is paging you. Do you raise the gateway timeout?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard trap question after any 5xx discussion.

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat a timeout as a deliberate budget or as an inconvenience to be tuned upward.

Not as a first move, and rarely as any move. A timeout is a decision about how long a caller is willing to hold a resource before giving up, and raising it does not make the backend faster — it makes each failing request occupy a connection, a worker and a slot in every upstream pool for longer. Under the load that produced the spike, that converts a bounded failure into resource exhaustion, and the 504s become 503s as pools fill. The timeout was doing its job; the thing behind it changed.

The correct sequence is to find what got slower. Compare the backend's own p99 against the timeout: if p99 crossed the threshold, you have a backend regression with a date on it, and the timeout merely reported it. If the backend's p99 is unchanged, the added time is between the hops — connection-pool waiting, a slow dependency, DNS — and a trace or a per-hop duration comparison locates it.

There is one legitimate reason to change it: the timeout was never derived from a budget in the first place. Timeouts should nest — each layer's shorter than its caller's, all of them from an end-to-end target rather than from a default that happens to be 30 or 60 seconds. And if the operation genuinely takes minutes, the fix is not a timeout at all but making it asynchronous.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

"Slow for only 2% of users" and every dashboard is green. Where do you go?

Green dashboards with a real complaint almost always mean the aggregate is hiding a segment, so the first move is to stop measuring and start segmenting: by region, by client version, by device class, by whether the connection was new or reused, and by tenant. A 2% cohort is invisible in a p99 across everyone and obvious in a p99 within its own group. Most of the time the segment names the cause outright — one region, one client build, one large tenant.

The specific resources that produce a small, persistent slow cohort are worth naming, because they are the ones dashboards miss. Cold connections: users whose sessions are short pay full DNS, TCP and TLS setup on every request, so the p99 for "new connection" requests can be 300 milliseconds while the reused-connection p99 is 40. One unhealthy instance still passing a shallow health check takes its share of traffic and serves it slowly; with 50 targets, that is 2%. A saturated per-tenant limit produces queueing for one customer only. A single stale DNS answer sends one region's clients to a decommissioned or distant endpoint until a TTL expires.

The failure presents as a disagreement between dashboards and support tickets. Server-side metrics look fine because they start measuring when the request arrives; the missing time is DNS, connection setup, or queueing at a hop that exports no duration. The gap closes with real-user monitoring for the client-side phases, per-instance rather than per-service latency, and traces filtered to the affected segment rather than sampled uniformly.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the observability for a streaming LLM product so these playbooks are executable in minutes rather than hours.

🎯 Really testing: whether you instrument the boundaries rather than the components, and whether you know which signals a streaming path needs that a request/response path does not.

The highest-stakes constraint is that a streaming response inverts the usual latency question. Total duration is meaningless — a long response should take a long time — so the metric that carries the product is time to first token, and the failure that hurts most is a hop that buffers, which does not raise the error rate or the total duration at all. Any design that only measures request duration and status code will be blind to the single most likely serious failure. So the first requirement is a first-byte metric emitted at every hop, and an alert on the gap between the edge's TTFB and the model service's.

The path is client → edge → load balancer → gateway → inference service → model, and the instrumentation goes at each boundary rather than inside each component. Every hop emits RED plus its own TTFB, plus the saturation signal that predicts its failure — pool usage at the gateway, accept-queue depth at the service, batch occupancy at the model. traceparent propagates end to end, and because a streaming request is one long span, each hop also emits a first-byte event inside it so the waterfall shows where the first token was delayed rather than only where the request ended. Long-lived connections need one thing request/response paths do not: an inventory of every idle timeout on the path, alerted on when any drops below the longest expected generation — an idle timeout shorter than a generation is why a stream dies at exactly 60 seconds.

The failure mode I would monitor first is buffering, precisely because it is silent. A synthetic canary that issues a streaming request every minute and records inter-token arrival gaps catches a newly-introduced buffering hop within a minute of a config change, and no other signal will — status codes stay 200, duration stays plausible, error rate stays zero. Second is connection-count saturation at the load balancer, since long-lived streams accumulate and hit per-LB limits long before CPU becomes interesting.

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The ordering principle behind every branch is eliminate the largest set first. A status code partitions the space in one step because it names the hop that formed the opinion. Where there is no code, the curl -w phase split partitions it in one command. Everything expensive — reading code, pulling traces, involving other teams — comes after both cheap partitions have run.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable this moves is time to mitigation, and it moves it by removing the part of an incident that is pure search. Most of the first twenty minutes of a live incident is spent deciding whose problem it is, and that decision is usually derivable from two commands nobody ran because everybody was reading dashboards. A written playbook converts that search into a lookup, and the difference shows up directly in incident duration.

It also matters because a wrong first hypothesis pulls in the wrong team, and a team pulled in wrongly twice responds slowly the third time. Playbooks protect the escalation path's credibility as much as they save minutes.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

The first ninety seconds of any of these playbooks, as an actual sequence:

# 1. WHAT is the symptom, precisely? Status code and which hop emitted it.
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'status=%{http_code} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total} proto=%{http_version} ip=%{remote_ip}\n' \
     https://api.example.com/v1/health

# 2. WHERE does the time go? The one command that partitions the suspects.
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "@$HOME/.curl-format.txt" https://api.example.com/v1/health

# 3. Is it ONE backend or all of them? Same hostname, pinned target.
for ip in 10.0.1.7 10.0.1.8 10.0.1.9; do
  printf '%-10s %s\n' "$ip" "$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_starttransfer}' \
    --resolve api.example.com:443:$ip https://api.example.com/v1/health)"
done

# 4. Streaming symptom? Does it trickle, or arrive in one burst at the end?
curl -N -sS https://api.example.com/v1/chat -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"stream":true}' \
  | while IFS= read -r l; do printf '%s %s\n' "$(date +%T.%3N)" "$l"; done

# 5. Resets or hangs? Count states on BOTH sides before theorising.
ss -s; ss -tan state close-wait | wc -l; ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l

9. Concrete Trace (Worked Decision Scenarios)

Scenario 1 — 503s on 40% of requests, application logs are silent. The silence is the clue rather than a gap: a 503 means the proxy found no healthy upstream, so the request never reached an application. Check the target-group health first — three of eight targets are failing. Check deploys second — a rollout started four minutes ago and the readiness probe path was changed in the same commit. Answer: the readiness probe, not the app. Defence: 503 is emitted before any upstream is attempted, which is exactly why nothing appears in application logs — the silence corroborates the code rather than contradicting it.

Scenario 2 — Intermittent 502s, roughly one request in 200, no pattern in time. 502 means something answered badly, so the upstream is alive. Check the proxy's error log for the specific reason — it says upstream prematurely closed connection. Check the two idle timeouts: the backend's keep-alive is 5 seconds, the proxy's upstream keep-alive is 60. Answer: a timeout mismatch. The proxy reuses a pooled connection the backend has already decided to close, loses the race, and the request dies mid-flight. Defence: the fix is making the downstream idle timeout strictly longer than the upstream's, so the side that pools is never the side that discovers the close.

Scenario 3 — "The dashboard is slow" from one office, fine everywhere else. Segment before measuring. curl -w from that office shows time_namelookup at 900 milliseconds while every other phase is normal; from another network it is 2 milliseconds. dig +trace returns the correct record quickly. Answer: the office's own resolver, not DNS and not the application. Defence: time_namelookup isolates resolution from everything downstream, and +trace proves the authoritative data is correct — which leaves only the resolver in between.

Scenario 4 — Token streaming works locally, arrives all at once in production. curl -N against production shows every line arriving in a single burst at t=8.2s; the same command against the service directly inside the VPC trickles correctly. That bisection puts the buffering hop between the edge and the service. Check each hop's buffering configuration in order — the CDN is fine, the gateway is fine, nginx has proxy_buffering on by default on the route added last week. Answer: the nginx hop. Defence: total ≈ starttransfer on a response that should stream is definitionally buffering, and running the same command from progressively deeper inside the network locates which hop does it.

Scenario 5 — Connections reset "randomly" at high load, no 5xx logged anywhere. No status code means no HTTP response, so the failure is below HTTP and no application will log it. ss -s on the client shows 27,000 sockets in TIME_WAIT, and the ephemeral port range is the default ~28,000. Answer: local ephemeral port exhaustion from unpooled outbound connections — it presents as the remote side refusing, while the remote side's dashboards are clean. Defence: the arithmetic is local and checkable — port range divided by TIME_WAIT duration gives the sustainable connection rate, and we are above it.

10. When TO Use This

  • At the start of every live incident, before opening a dashboard — the playbook's first two checks are cheaper than the first dashboard query and eliminate more.

  • When you are the one being escalated to and need to decide in a minute whether this is yours. The 5xx table alone usually settles ownership.

  • When onboarding someone onto an on-call rotation. Playbooks are the transferable part of debugging experience; the intuition underneath them is not.

  • When writing a postmortem action item. "Add a playbook entry for this symptom" is a durable fix that survives the people who were on the call, unlike "we'll remember to check the idle timeout."

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not run a playbook past the point where it stops discriminating. These are branch-eliminators, not root-cause finders. Once the branch is narrowed to one hop, switch to that hop's own tools — profiles, traces, code.

  • Do not follow a playbook when you already have a strong, specific signal. If a deploy went out ninety seconds before the spike, roll it back and investigate afterwards. The playbook is for when you do not know; mitigation always outranks diagnosis.

  • Do not let the playbook substitute for understanding the mechanism. Someone who has memorised "503 means health checks" without knowing why will be lost the moment a load balancer emits 503 for a connection limit instead. The tables compress knowledge you should already hold.

  • Do not keep a playbook you have not re-run since the architecture changed. A stale playbook is worse than none, because it is followed confidently. Adding a service mesh or a new edge changes which hop emits which code, and the table has to change with it.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A 502 means the backend is down."

✅ Reality: 502 means the proxy got a response it could not use — a connection closed mid-response, a protocol mismatch, oversized headers. Something was alive and answering. "Down" produces a 503, because there is no healthy upstream to try at all. Reading 502 as "down" sends you to look at capacity when the evidence points at a single request's handling.

❌ Misconception: "Raising the timeout fixes the 504s."

✅ Reality: It converts fast failures into slow ones and holds connections, workers and pool slots for longer under exactly the load that caused the spike — which typically turns 504s into 503s as pools fill. The number to change is whatever made the backend slower; the timeout merely reported it.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Silent application logs during a 5xx spike mean the logging is broken."

✅ Reality: For 503 the silence is the expected, corroborating evidence — the proxy never forwarded the request, so no application could have logged it. Treating silence as a second problem doubles the search space at the worst possible moment, when it was actually the strongest confirmation of the first hypothesis.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Answering "server error" and stopping. 502, 503 and 504 are three different accusations from the same accuser. Collapsing them into one category discards the only free information the incident gave you, and it is the single most common shallow answer on this topic.

Naming a tool instead of a decision tree. "I'd check the logs" is not triage. Which logs, in what order, and what would each outcome eliminate? The value is in the ordering — cheapest, most-discriminating check first — and someone who cannot articulate the ordering is describing a habit rather than a method.

Skipping segmentation on a "slow for some users" report. Reaching for an aggregate p99 when the complaint is explicitly about a subset guarantees a green dashboard and a stalled investigation. The first move is to split the population, not to measure it.

Forgetting who is in the middle. Answering as if the path were client-to-server when there are three proxies, a CDN and a service mesh between them skips every hop where these symptoms actually originate. Buffering, idle timeouts, header limits and health checks all live in the middle.

Confidently quoting a default you have not checked. "The ALB times out at 60 seconds" may not be true of the configuration in front of you; defaults change and are routinely overridden. Say where the number comes from, or say you would check it.

Stopping at the happy path. A check with no defined next step for "came back clean" is a hunch with a command attached, not a branch.

16. Real World Usage

Every mature on-call rotation ships playbooks with the alert. The pattern that works is a link in the alert payload straight to the symptom's entry, so the responder does not have to identify the symptom before finding the guidance — the alert has already done that classification.

The Cloudflare 2019 outage is the canonical case for the "eliminate the largest set first" ordering: a single regular expression in a WAF rule saturated CPU globally, and the decisive early observation was that the failure was universal across customers and regions rather than segment-specific. That partition — everyone versus a segment — is the top branch of the flowchart above, and it is what pointed at a global config push rather than any customer's traffic.

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

The framing is operational rather than architectural: "you shipped this, it is 3am, users say the product is slow — what do you do?" It is a design question in disguise, because answering it well means describing a system instrumented at its boundaries. A beautiful topology whose author cannot say which hop reports the first symptom is a system nobody can operate, and that is what is being probed.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10x traffic Trace volume and metric cardinality outgrow the collector; per-hop labels multiply Head-sample low, tail-sample errors and outliers; prune unbounded labels
100x traffic Per-instance latency series become too many to query; one bad target hides in aggregates Exemplars linking metrics to traces; per-target histograms retained short, aggregates long
1000x traffic Playbooks stop scaling to a human — too many hops to check by hand Automate the top branches: correlate deploys, segment automatically, attach the candidate hop to the alert

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • At 10x, the "check every hop" step exceeds the time budget of an incident, and the first metric to degrade is time-to-mitigation even though every component is healthy.

  • At 100x, aggregate dashboards stop being able to represent a segment at all, so "slow for some users" becomes permanently invisible without automated segmentation.

  • Operationally, the thing that wakes you at 3am is a playbook that was accurate six months ago and now names a hop that no longer emits that code — followed confidently, and wrong.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • RED at every hop, with TTFB as a first-class metric on streaming routes. Alert on the gap between adjacent hops' durations rather than on any single hop's absolute value — the gap is what names an owner.

  • Saturation signals with no graceful degradation get pages: accept-queue drops and ephemeral-port exhaustion. Both present as connection failures that never reach application logs, so a symptom alert would arrive only via a user.

  • A streaming canary measuring inter-token arrival gaps, every minute. It is the only signal that detects a newly-introduced buffering hop, because status codes, error rate and total duration all stay healthy while it happens.
